'''wanwit†''', ''n.'' [ME. ''wanwit'' (= G. ''wahnwitz'' = Sw. ''vanvett'' = Dan. ''vanvid''); < ''wan-'' + ''wit.''] Lack of sense; foolishness.
{{smaller block|<poem>Schild me from pein of helle pit,

{{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 180.}}}}

'''wany†''', ''v.'' A Middle English form of ''wane''<sup>2</sup>.

'''wanyand†''', ''n.'' Same as ''waniand.''

'''wanze†''', ''v. i.'' See ''wanse.''

'''wap'''<sup>1</sup> (wop), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''wapped'', ppr. ''wapping.'' [< ME. ''wappen''; cf. ''whap'', ''whop'', and ''quap''<sup>1</sup>, ''quop''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To strike; knock; beat; wallop; drub. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|Why, either of my boys could ''wap'' him with one hand.
{{right|''Thackeray.''}}}}
'''2.''' To flap; flutter. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>There ’s nae a cock in a’ the land
But has ''wappit'' its wings and crawn.</poem>
{{right|''Glasgerian'' (Allingham’s Ballad-book), p. 361.}}}}
'''3.''' To toss or throw quickly. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Tak a halter in thy hose,
And o’ thy purpose dinna fail;
But ''wap'' it o’er the Wanton’s nose.</poem>
{{right|''Lochmaben Harper'' (Child’s Ballads, VI. 4).}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To flutter; flap the wings; move violently. [Obsolete or provincial.]

'''wap'''<sup>1</sup> (wop), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wappe''; < ''wap''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] A smart stroke; a blow. [Obsolete or provincial.]

[Sc., also ''wappenshaw'', ''wapinschaw'', etc., lit. ‘weapon-show,’ < ''wapen'' (a form of ''weapon'') + ''shaw.''] A show or review of persons under arms, formerly made at certain times in every district. {{smaller|These exhibitions or meetings were not designed for military exercises, but only to show that the lieges were properly provided with arms. {{right|''Scott'', Old Mortality, vii.}}}}

Ill brought up; undisciplined; unrestrained; hence, free from moral control. {{smaller block|He . . . associate vnto hym certeyn ''wanton'' persones, & bete his mayster. {{right|''Fabyan'', Chron., cxxvii.}}}} '''2.''' Characterized by extreme recklessness, foolhardiness, or heartlessness; malicious; recklessly disregardful of right or of consequences: applied both to persons and to their acts. {{smaller block|The ''wanton'' troopers riding by Have shot my fawn, and it will dye. {{right|''Marvell'', Nymph Complaining for Death of her Fawn.}}}} '''3.''' Wild; unruly; loose; unrestrained. {{smaller block|And take good hede bi wisdom & resoun That bi no ''wantowne'' lauȝinge thou do noon offence To-fore thi souereyne while he is in presence. {{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 27.}}}} {{smaller block|She, as a veil, down to the slender waist Her unadorned golden tresses wore Dishevel’d, but in ''wanton'' ringlets waved. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 304.}}}} {{smaller block|How does your tongue grow ''wanton'' in her praise! {{right|''Addison'', Cato, i. 5.}}}} '''4.''' Playful; sportive; frolicsome. {{smaller block|All ''wanton'' as a child, skipping and vain. {{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 771.}}}} {{smaller block|Ye valleys low, where the mild whispers rise Of shades, and ''wanton'' winds, and gushing brooks. {{right|''Milton'', Lycidas, l. 136.}}}} '''5.''' Rank; luxuriant. {{smaller block|The quaint mazes in the ''wanton'' green. {{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., ii. 1. 99.}}}} {{smaller block|Every ungovernable passion grows ''wanton'' and luxuriant in corrupt religions. {{right|''Bacon'', Fable of Dionysius.}}}} '''6.''' Characterized by unrestrained indulgence of the natural impulses or appetites; dissolute; licentious. {{smaller block|The proud day, Attended with the pleasures of the world, Is all too ''wanton'' and too full of gawds. {{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iii. 3. 36.}}}} {{smaller block|Men, grown ''wanton'' by prosperity, Study’d new arts of luxury and ease. {{right|''Roscommon'', tr. of Horace’s Art of Poetry.}}}} {{smaller block|''Wanton'' professor and damnable apostate. {{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, i.}}}} '''7.''' Particularly, unchaste; lascivious; libidinous; lustful; lewd. {{smaller block|Thou art . . . froward by nature, enemy to peace, Lascivious, ''wanton.'' ''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., iii. 1. 19.}} {{smaller block|A ''wanton'' mistress is a common sewer. {{right|''Ford'', Lady’s Trial, i. 2.}}}} '''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A pampered, petted creature; one spoiled by fondness or indulgence; also, a frolicsome, roving, sportive creature; a trifler: used sometimes as a term of endearment. {{smaller block|Thy parents made thee a ''wanton'' with too much cockering. {{right|''Lyly'', Euphues, Anat. of Wit, p. 36.}}}} {{smaller block|Shall a beardless boy, A cocker’d silken ''wanton'', brave our fields? {{right|''Shak.'', K. John, v. 1. 70.}}}} '''2.''' A lewd person; a lascivious man or woman. {{smaller block|If ye be set on pleasure, or disposed to ''wantons'', ye shall have ministers enough to be furtherers and instruments of it. {{right|''Latimer'', 2d Sermon bef. To revel; frolic unrestrainedly; sport. {{smaller block|When, like some childish wench, she loosely ''wantoning'' With tricks and giddy turns seems to inisle the shore. {{right|''Drayton'', Polyolbion, ii. 174.}}}} {{smaller block|Nature here ''Wanton’d'' as in her prime. ''Milton'', P. L., v. 294.}} {{smaller block|Her cap-strings ''wantoned'' in front of her in the rising wind. {{right|''Mrs. Oliphant'', May, ii.}}}} '''2.''' To sport or dally in lewdness; sport lasciviously. '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To make wanton. {{smaller block|If he does win, it ''wantons'' him with over-plus, and enters him into new ways of expence. {{right|''Feltham'', Resolves, ii. 58.}}}} '''2.'''
